## The question

[Maclaurin series of $f(x)= e^{-x}\sin(x)$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5086742/maclaurin-series-of-fx-e-x-sinx), asked by [Person](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1670719/person) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2025-07-30; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> $$f(x)=e^{-x}\sin x$$
>
> I tried applying Cauchy product, but I'm not sure if using Cauchy product was the correct choice. It said that I need one absolute convergence. I had tried and my answer was : 
> $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty }\sum_{n=0}^{k}\frac{(-1)^k x^{2k+1}}{x^{n}n!(2(k-n)+1)!}$$
> My process steps were:
>
> $$e^{-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{x^n(-1)^n}{n!}$$
>
> $$sin(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{x^{2j+1}(-1)^{j}}{(2j+1)!}$$
>
> So
> $$c_k=\sum_{n=0}^{k}\frac{x^n(-1)^n}{n!}. \frac{x^{2(k-n)+1}(-1)^{(k-n)}}{(2(k-n)+1)!}$$
> then i change it into
> $$c_k=\sum_{n=0}^{k}\frac{x^n(-1)^n}{n!}. \frac{x^{2k-2n+1}(-1)^{k}}{(2(k-n)+1)!(-1)^n}$$
> and then $$c_k=\sum_{n=0}^{k}\frac{x^n(-1)^n}{n!}. \frac{x^{2k+1}(-1)^{k}}{x^{2n}(2(k-n)+1)!(-1)^n}$$
>
> After that I cancel out the term and it lead me to my current answer
> $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty }\sum_{n=0}^{k}\frac{(-1)^k x^{2k+1}}{x^{n}n!(2(k-n)+1)!}$$
>
>
> Please go easy on me guys, I tried searching for the answer and explanation but I couldn't found it:(
>
> If i did something wrong please point out and explain to me, thank you for helping me.
>
> Thank you for all your effort guys, i will study complex number after i'm done with my material. I think it's better to take the process slow to gain a better understanding, hope you guys can understand!
:::

I wanted to build off Utsabraj Sarkar's answer and complete the complex binomial method. For OP: The only thing you need to know about complex numbers is that $i$ is a number satisfying $i^2=-1$. Other than that, it behaves just like a real number.

We have $$e^{-x}\sin x=\frac{1}{2i}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\,\left[\frac{(i-1)^n-(-1)^n(i+1)^n}{n!}\right]x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n$$

Using the binomial theorem twice,
$$\begin{align*}
   a_n &= \frac{1}{2i\,n!}\left\{ \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} i^k (-1)^{n-k} - (-1)^n \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} i^k 1^{n-k}\right\}
\\&= \frac{(-1)^n}{2i\, n!} \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} i^k \left((-1)^{-k} - 1 \right)
\end{align*}$$
Now powers of $-1$ alternate between $\pm1$, depending on whether the exponent is even or odd. So
$$\left((-1)^{-k} - 1\right) = \begin{cases} 
        0 & \text{if $k$ is even} \\
       -2 & \text{if $k$ is odd} \end{cases}$$
This means we can ignore all the even $k$ and only sum over odd $k$. An odd number $k$ can be written as $2j+1$, where $j$ is another natural number. 
Also, $i^{2j+1} = i^{2j} i = (-1)^j i$. Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}
    a_n &= \frac{(-1)^n}{2i\, n!} \sum_{0 \leq 2j+1 \leq n} \binom{n}{2j+1} i^{2j+1} (-2) 
    \\&= \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!} \sum_{0 \leq 2j+1 \leq n} \binom{n}{2j+1}(-1)^j
\end{align*}$$
Although the notation is intimidating, the summation itself is not too bad. You take the alternating sum of binomial coefficients with $n$ on top and increasing odd numbers in the bottom. You could also write it as:
$$a_n = \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!} \left[ \binom{n}{1} - \binom{n}{3} + \binom{n}{5} - \dots \right]$$
understanding that the sum is finite because the terms are eventually zero.

To write out the first few terms:
$$\begin{align*}
    a_0 &= 0 \text{ (because the sum is empty)}
\\
    a_1 &= \frac{(-1)^2}{1!} \left[\binom{1}{1} \right] = 1
\\
    a_2 &= -\frac{1}{2!} \left[\binom{2}{1}\right] = -1
\\
    a_3 &= \frac{1}{3!} \left[\binom{3}{1} - \binom{3}{3} \right] = \frac{1}{6} (3-1) = \frac{1}{3}
\\
    a_4 &= -\frac{1}{4!} \left[\binom{4}{1} - \binom{4}{3}\right] = 0
\\
    a_5 &= \frac{1}{5!} \left[\binom{5}{1} - \binom{5}{3} + \binom{5}{5} \right] = \frac{1}{120} \left(5-10+1\right) = -\frac{4}{120} = -\frac{1}{30}
\\
    a_6 &= -\frac{1}{6!} \left[\binom{6}{1} - \binom{6}{3} + \binom{6}{5} \right] = -\frac{1}{720} \left(6-20+6\right) = \frac{8}{720} = \frac{1}{90}
\end{align*}$$
This agrees with [Wolfram Alpha](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=maclaurin+series+for+e%5E%28-x%29+sin%28x%29).
